title: Git Essentials: Commands & Concepts
description: The everyday Git commands and ideas you need to track changes, work with branches, and collaborate through a remote.
subject: computer-science

cards.definition: Holds the snapshot of changes that will go into the next commit. You add changes to it with git add.
Replays your commits on top of a different base commit, producing a linear history. The replayed commits get new hashes.
Shelves your uncommitted changes to tracked files so you can work on something else and reapply them later.
Creates a new, empty Git repository in the current directory.
Copies an existing repository, including its full history, and sets up a remote named origin.
Stages changes from the working tree so they are included in the next commit.
Records the staged snapshot in history, along with a message, the author, and a link to its parent commit.
Shows which files are staged, which are modified but unstaged, and which are untracked.
Shows line-by-line changes. With no arguments, it compares the working tree to the staging area.
Lists the commit history, newest first by default.
A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit that advances automatically as you commit on it.
A reference to the commit you currently have checked out, usually by way of the current branch.
HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch, so any new commits you make don't belong to a branch.
Brings another branch's changes into the current branch, creating a merge commit unless a fast-forward is possible.
A merge where the current branch has no commits of its own since the branches split, so Git just moves its pointer ahead.
Happens when two branches change the same lines differently and Git can't combine them automatically, so you resolve it by hand.
A named reference to another copy of the repository, such as origin, that you fetch from and push to.
Downloads new commits and branch updates from a remote without changing your local branches or working tree.
Fetches from a remote and then integrates the changes into the current branch, by merging or rebasing.
Uploads the commits on your local branch to a remote repository.
Creates a new commit that undoes the changes from an earlier commit, without rewriting history.
Moves the current branch to a given commit and discards all staged and unstaged changes to tracked files.
Applies the changes from a specific existing commit onto the current branch as a new commit.
A file of patterns for untracked files Git should ignore. It has no effect on files that are already tracked.
